blocks.text: Jenny put a clean sheet into her typewriter, then took it out again. She had begun with the locked chair. First, she needed to explain why she had gone there.

On her desk lay the campaign invitation, her questions about the electricity supply and the notes she had made after the escape. The police had taken statements. She and Super Zerdo had described the gas and the restraints; Billy had described what he had heard from the yard, his punch and Luke carrying Daniel away. They had all stayed to answer questions after help arrived.
Jenny read the invitation against her account, line by line, then checked Daniel’s words against her notes.
Her editor drew up a chair. Jenny kept her hand on her notes. Billy had found Eleanor beside this man’s telephone. The earlier call still had no explanation.
“Will you judge this account on what I can document?” she asked.
“Check it, and we’ll print it,” he said. He pointed to her notes. “Tell me about the lights again.”
“Four bulbs. A cable to a storage unit. He said the source would come later.”
“So he showed you stored electricity being used.”
“Exactly.” She crossed out a sentence and wrote another above it. “He didn’t show me anything that could power Cleveland.”
She described the unfinished collector as she had seen it, with loose wiring and nobody inside. Daniel’s claims about what it might do went into quotation marks. They were his claims, not results.

Jenny telephoned the landlord to check the payment history against the invoice. Then she called Eleanor’s campaign office. She read out the details she intended to report: the demonstration, the interview invitation, the rent and what had happened to the two prisoners. “Why was her campaign working with Daniel after the robot attack?” she asked. “And why send a reporter to his laboratory?” She asked for Eleanor’s response and kept both questions in her account.
“When do you need it?” the aide asked.
Jenny gave the newsroom deadline and her telephone number. “If she disputes anything, I want to hear it.”

The reply came while the editor was reading her second draft. The campaign said Eleanor had expected a scientific interview and had not authorized anyone’s detention. Jenny wrote down the statement, read it back and included it. No test results came with it.
“Do we say she knew?” the editor asked, tapping the account of the kidnapping.

“Her office arranged the interview and promoted his work,” Jenny said. “That doesn’t show she knew he would imprison us. The rent payments don’t tell us she knowingly paid for the robot, either. Billy’s question about the order holding back the police is still unanswered.”
The editor nodded. “Then we say what we have.”

Jenny checked the photograph caption last. SUPER ZERDO. Under the headline was her own byline, Jenny Jenkins. The account named Dr. Daniel Orkleson as the man who had gassed and imprisoned her and Super Zerdo. It described how the masked hero and his allies had helped free her. It gave no civilian name for him, and nothing that connected her to the pink figure in the earlier photographs.

By the time Jenny walked past the corner newsstand, the seller was holding up the Defender. FREE ELECTRICITY PROMISE EXPOSED ran across the page. A man stopped, bought a copy and stood beside the stand to read past the headline.
blocks.alt: A Cleveland newspaper seller holds up the Defender with the headline “Free Electricity Promise Exposed,” Jenny Jenkins’s byline and a photograph captioned Super Zerdo.

blocks.text: The story did not empty Eleanor’s meeting halls that morning. People still wanted lower bills. Some said she deserved time to explain. Others wanted to see the equipment for themselves.
Over the remaining weeks of the campaign, those questions kept coming.
At a neighborhood meeting, a woman waited until Eleanor had finished talking about street repairs. Then she raised her hand.
“Has anybody independent made your electricity system work yet?”
Eleanor said the research had suffered a setback. Her office would provide more information when it was ready.
Jenny wrote down the answer. The following day, she called for the information.

There was no working system to show her. No convincing independent results arrived at the Defender or at the other newspapers asking for them. At one meeting, an aide gathered unused handbills from the empty chairs. At another, Eleanor tried to move on to a different subject, and three people asked her to finish answering the first one.
Jenny kept reporting the answers she received, including the ones that amounted to another request for time. The promise stayed on the posters. Fewer people seemed willing to take it home.
On election night, Billy left his office radio on. Seth sat beside Jenny while the reports came in. Fist rested on a folded cloth, listening with his eyes half closed.
They waited through the announcer’s pauses and the rustle of fresh papers. Then came the result. Eleanor Blackwell had lost.

At campaign headquarters, supporters stood when Eleanor approached the microphone. Their applause faded before she put her notes on the podium. Claude waited nearby, looking tired. He had come to stand beside his wife; the arrangement with Daniel had never been his.
Eleanor thanked the people who had worked for her. She thanked the voters who had placed their trust in her. For a few sentences, she sounded as smooth as she had on the City Hall steps.
Then a reporter asked whether the electricity promise had cost her that trust.
“I put my faith in a scientist,” she said. “I expected him to deliver work that would benefit this city. He failed to do so.”
She lifted her notes. One corner crumpled beneath her thumb.
“Dr. Orkleson assured us he could deliver. After what he has put this city through, perhaps ‘Doc Dork’ would be more fitting.”
blocks.alt: Eleanor, in her black suit, pearls and dark glasses, delivers her concession speech with notes in one hand. Claude stands nearby before subdued supporters.

blocks.text: A few supporters laughed uncertainly. Claude looked at her, but said nothing. Eleanor smoothed the paper against the podium and returned to thanking her campaign staff.
In Billy’s office, Seth looked up from the radio.
“She picked him,” he said.
“And made the promise,” Jenny said. She had written down Eleanor’s exact words.

The following morning, the newspapers printed them. One headline carried the election result; another repeated the insult beside Daniel’s photograph. By the time the Defender’s copies reached the newsroom, someone at the next desk was reading the phrase aloud.

Jenny laid the paper flat. There was Daniel behind his enormous glasses, with Eleanor’s “DOC DORK” remark above him. Beneath it, the report set out her claim that she had trusted him, and the questions her campaign had never answered.
blocks.alt: The morning newspaper repeats Eleanor’s “Doc Dork” remark beside a photograph of Daniel beneath its report of her election defeat.

blocks.text: “She’s given them something easier to remember than Orkleson,” the editor said.
Jenny looked at the photograph. “They still need to remember what he did.”

That evening, Eleanor’s sitting-room telephone rang. Campaign papers lay beside her chair, and she still wore her dark glasses. When she heard Daniel’s voice, she sat down without inviting him to continue.
“I heard your speech,” he said.
“Then you know what your promises have cost me.”
“You didn’t have to call me that.”
“I didn’t have to spend a campaign explaining why you could light four bulbs and nothing else.”
Daniel tightened his grip on the receiver. Beside him, Luke hovered silently.
“I could finish the work,” Daniel said. “With some assistance. The rent alone—”
“No.”
“You haven’t heard what I need.”
“No more funding. No rent money. No assistance.” Eleanor’s voice sharpened. “You have damaged my campaign enough. Our arrangement is finished.”
“If you would give me time—”
She put down the receiver. Daniel kept his at his ear until Luke spoke.
blocks.alt: In a split scene, Eleanor ends the telephone call in her sitting room while Daniel grips his receiver beside bodyless Luke against an unidentified plain background.

blocks.text: “Is she going to help?”
“No.”
Luke looked at him. “You said you could finish.”
Daniel lowered the telephone. For once, Luke did not ask him when.

A few days after the election, Billy and Jenny went back to the basement with the landlord. The police had already photographed the workshop and collected the collector, papers, damaged cage and restraints as evidence. They had permitted the landlord to enter with them. Jenny left the remaining fixtures alone.

They went down the yard steps, through the service door and past the front-room sink. The shelf was still rolled clear of the inner doorway. Beyond it, bare patches marked where Daniel’s equipment had stood.
Without the machinery’s hum, Billy could hear a pipe ticking overhead. The high window showed the yard wall. Jenny stopped beside the doorway rather than going to the place where her chair had been.
“No more rent,” the landlord said. “No message. He hasn’t come back.” Billy looked across the empty bench. There was no forwarding address, and nothing to say where Daniel and Luke had settled.
blocks.alt: Billy, civilian Jenny and the gray-bearded landlord look into the dry basement workshop after police have removed its equipment as evidence; pipes and a small high window remain.

blocks.text: “Will you let the police know if he contacts you?” Jenny asked.
The landlord nodded. “I’ve already told them I will.”
Outside, Billy waited while he locked the service door. Jenny climbed the steps slowly beside him. She was glad to reach the street.

By the time Seth arrived at Billy’s office that afternoon, the lamp was on. He wore his orange hoodie, with the sleeves pushed back from his hands. Jenny had brought the Defender. Billy made space for it between the folders and the telephone.
“Anything?” Seth asked.
“Neither of them has returned,” Billy said. “The police have our accounts and the evidence from the workshop. We’ll tell them if we learn more.”
Seth sat down. “And Eleanor?”
“She won’t be mayor,” Billy said. “But she still has money, and people who take her calls.”
Jenny folded the newspaper. “We’ve reported what we know about her campaign. We still can’t show she knew about the kidnapping.”
“Her threats made me careful,” Billy said. “They didn’t stop me telling the police what happened.” He closed his notebook and drew his chair nearer the others.

Fist shifted on the cushion beside the lamp. The scuffed leather still creased when he moved, and his torn cuff lay carefully supported. Billy adjusted the cushion’s edge until the glove settled comfortably again.
“Better?”
“Better.” Fist opened both eyes. “You can stop watching me now.”
Billy moved his chair back an inch. “I’m looking at the newspaper.”
“Sure you are.”
Beside the open window, Flaming Head’s flames curled in the evening air. The curtain was drawn well back, and Billy had moved the papers clear. Warmth reached Seth with a quiet message.
“He says we can leave practice until everyone’s ready,” Seth told Billy and Fist.
“Good,” Fist said. “Tomorrow I’m practicing this.” He settled deeper into the cushion.
Jenny smiled. “I can come by after work. Shall I bring sandwiches?”
Billy opened his appointment book. “I’ll put the kettle on.”
“What time?” Seth asked.
“Six?” Jenny looked at him. “Will you be here?”
“I’ll be here.”

Seth leaned back beside her, smiling. Jenny’s newspaper lay in the circle of lamplight. Across the desk, Billy wrote six in his book while Fist offered an opinion about the sandwiches. Flaming Head stayed by the window. “I’ll be here tomorrow, too,” he told Seth and Jenny.
blocks.alt: Civilian Seth smiles beside Jenny in Billy’s warmly lit office. Billy sits at his desk, injured Fist rests on a cushion, and Flaming Head hovers safely beside the open window.

blocks.text: “I’d hoped so,” Jenny said. Seth passed the message to Billy and Fist. Then he remembered something he had meant to tell Billy, and Billy put down his pencil to listen.
Outside, a bus pulled away from the stop. Seth could have caught it if he left now. There would be another one.
He stayed a little longer, happy in the company of his friends.
